notes.heading: A measurement model must include the vessel and its uncertainty
paragraphs: Mass comparisons require a consistent system boundary and a clear tare procedure. A vessel's mass is subtracted from the combined reading to obtain the sample mass. If the same stable additive balance offset affects both readings, it can cancel in the difference, though it would still bias either absolute reading. This does not remove all uncertainty: resolution, drift, sample loss and changed conditions may remain. When uncertainty rules are supplied in a problem, use those rules explicitly instead of treating one classroom convention as universal.

questions.prompt: A balance consistently reads 0.20 g too high. The empty vessel reads 50.20 g and the vessel plus sample reads 53.70 g. Find the sample mass by subtraction and explain what happens to the constant offset.
questions.answer: The sample mass is 3.50 g; the same +0.20 g offset cancels in the difference.
solution: Subtract the empty-vessel reading from the combined reading.
Express the readings as true masses plus the same offset to show cancellation; changing drift would not necessarily cancel.
markingPoints: Explain cancellation of the shared offset.
State that stable equal offsets are required.

questions.prompt: An idealised closed reaction vessel initially contains 12.0 g of reactants. After reaction, 7.5 g is solid and 1.2 g is liquid, with no other materials. Find the gas mass and explain why ignoring the gas gives an apparent loss.
questions.answer: Gas mass is 3.3 g. Counting only solid and liquid omits part of the closed system.
solution: Use total final mass equal to 12.0 g.
markingPoints: Use conservation for the closed system.

questions.prompt: Two independent readings are 10.0±0.1 g and 3.0±0.1 g. Using the stated worst-case bound method, find the difference and its uncertainty.
solution: Extreme differences range from 9.9-3.1=6.8 to 10.1-2.9=7.2 g.
markingPoints: State ±0.2 g under the specified method.
